Reading passage:
Software testing has evolved from a manual, repetitive activity into a discipline that relies heavily on automation.
Automated tests can run thousands of checks overnight, giving developers quick feedback on every change. Yet
automation is not a magic cure. Poorly designed scripts break whenever the interface changes, and teams then
spend more time repairing tests than writing new ones. Experienced engineers therefore automate only stable,
high-value scenarios and leave exploratory work, which depends on human curiosity, to manual testers.

What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Automation has replaced all manual testing
Automation is valuable but should be applied selectively

Reading passage:
Large language models generate text by predicting likely words, not by looking up verified facts. As a result, they
can produce confident answers that are completely wrong, a problem often called hallucination. Testing such
systems is different from testing traditional software because the same question can yield slightly different
answers each time. Testers therefore design evaluation sets, check answers against trusted sources and look
for biased or unsafe outputs. No single test can guarantee perfect behaviour.

According to the passage, why do language models hallucinate?
options: They are connected to the internet
They predict likely words rather than look up verified facts

transfer that debits one account but fails to credit another leaves the books unbalanced. Database testers
therefore verify that data remains accurate, consistent and complete after every operation. They write queries to
compare stored values with expected results, check that rules such as unique account numbers are enforced
and ensure that failed transactions are rolled back cleanly.
